event: VXE 448 (MARSOC, deployed) self-aborted VTOL launch two or three times on 1 March 2025, once at 20 to 30 ft and once at 300 ft as the cruise motor started, and returned to land; a launch on 3 March was normal.

contributing: very noisy RF environment at the deployed site
LRF fault logged as a side effect of being outside its operating range
HD55 payload in use

evidence.quote: there was a  vtol fault during climb, RTLdebugMsg Climb abort, VTOL controller fault followed by a sensor: GPS fault
Suspect GPS interference. Will update with some plots this afternoon or tomorrow. Exceeded some accuracy checks during VTOL climb
No jammers that I know of. RF all over the place it’s very noisy in this area
it seems likely the LRF fault is going to occur anytime we’re outside of it’s operational range and one of the other faults trips
This has been reported previously as most likely interference in the GPS L1 band in the area of

team_root_cause: Probable RF Signal interference led to U-Blox receiver performance / accuracy estimate indicators exceeding limits and causing launch abort.

would_settle_it.what: GPS accuracy estimate and C/N0 traces against the launch abort thresholds during each VTOL climb
Vehicle Investigation VXEP-1066.pptx slides naming which GPS accuracy threshold tripped on each abort

would_settle_it.what: confirm an L1 band interference source near the launch point, as was done for ENG-3018

reasoning: The XCOMM event log quoted in the comments shows a GPS sensor fault during VTOL climb that tripped the climb abort, with the LRF fault following as a side effect. Engineers found GPS accuracy checks exceeded and the customer described a very noisy RF area, and the same aircraft flew normally two days later. This is a designed abort on a degraded GPS input, so it is narrowed to GPS with the interference source unproven.
notes: GCS log notes suggest three aborts on 1 March, not the two reported. The event log cited is named XC250303.txt although the aborts were reported for 1 March. ENG-3018 is an older MARSOC GPS interference case at a different site, used only as context. No converted attachments on this ticket; all six are archives or images.

event: After Mod-A kit retrofits for PMA-263, Bloodhound testing at Dam Neck found the right QB antenna 30 to 56 dB down, non-captive MAIM fasteners, an AHRS PPS failure and DSUB screws backing out; no aircraft incident.
component: wing tip array antenna mount contact holder and RF cable assembly (PN 111-105524)
position: right wing tip antenna (Bloodhound QB array)
failure_mode: SMPM contacts not extended far enough: nominal contact interference below what the SMPM connection needs, giving a poor RF mate and large signal loss
contributing: field shims and tape did not restore the mate
MAIM Micro-D screws not captive (VA-2521)
AHRS PPS output set to an unsupported mode and 1 us pulse in MAIM firmware (VXEP-1138)
DSUB 4-40 hardware installed backwards and standoff peg about 1/16 inch too long

evidence.quote: I looked at the array mount interface and found that the nominal contact interference is less than the SMPM connection should have.
This most likely contributes to the poor connection and dB drop we see.
Summary: right antenna reported between 30-56 dB difference from center and left
While shims and new holders improve contact, they do not fully resolve the issue.
The AHRS spec calls out a feature that is unsupported with the version of AHRS firmware we have been running.
Screws often would fall out of connector in the field when operators were uninstalling harness, making them easy to lose.

team_view_in_comments: the nominal contact interference is less than the SMPM connection should have.  This most likely contributes to the poor connection and dB drop we see.

Bloodhound right antenna dB delta with the new contact holder and RF cable assembly from VA-2533

Matt Weber's analysis of the mount found contact interference below the SMPM requirement, and VA-2533 redesigned the contact holder and cable assembly for that reason. The other three issues each have their own cause in linked tickets and are listed as contributing.
notes: One ticket covers four separate kit problems; Issue 1 (RF cabling misalignment) is taken as the main one. The AHRS PPS issue was traced in VXEP-1138 to MAIM firmware setting an unsupported PPS mode and a 1 us pulse, fixed in MAIM_v30108. The two attached PDFs are identical. Parent projects VA-2455 and VXEP-891 were not read. Position is the right wing tip antenna, not a motor.

event: On VXE 557 (USASOC) on 12 Oct 2024, after an RTB at 32% the main battery state shown in flight swung between 16 and 30% from IP1 to IP4; the aircraft landed safely showing 30% and the charger later read 12%.
component: FWAP battery state of charge model (CalcVBLife, VLife)
failure_mode: voltage-based SoC estimate, built from an unloaded battery table and tuned for about 400 W and 30 A, swings when the load is outside that range during approach and landing
contributing: low log sampling rate
charger or checker SoC not reliable for the main battery (VXEP-762)
possible VTOL current or grounding effect on the voltage used (VXEP-761 comment)

evidence.quote: The fluctuation in the Battery State, as described in the customer’s report, can be attributed to an inaccurate SoC model that was modeled for loads of 400W and 30A.
The investigation report highlights 2 other flights from Flight Ops that show Battery State fluctuating when the load is outside of the 400W and 30A range.
One thing to note is that the model is based off an unloaded battery.
Logs do not show any explicate signs of  a bad mating connection - Voltage and current dropping simultaneously.
Thanks @Eric Brewer this seems like pretty clear correlation that inaccuracy is due to VTOL current/grounding issues.

team_root_cause:
- Caused by AS150 damage/systemic issue. Tracked here. https://jenaero.atlassian.net/browse/VXEP-761 and here https://jenaero.atlassian.net/browse/VXEP-553
- Inaccurate SoC Model caused the fluctuation of Battery State on OCT 12th
- Logs do not show any explicate signs of  a bad mating connection - Voltage and current dropping simultaneously.
- VLife - Main Battery State in the Logs - shows a large fluctuation when the load is out of the 400W and 30A range. This was also seen on different flights not related to this vehicle

would_settle_it.what: SoC captured by the vehicle against the battery model and the desired model for the 12 Oct flight
VLife against load power and current through IP1 to IP4
VXEP-761 flight logs: main battery voltage and VTOL current during the fluctuation

reasoning: The data review found nothing abnormal in voltage and current and no sign of a bad battery mate on 12 Oct, but the logged VLife battery state swings whenever load leaves the 400 W and 30 A region, and two unrelated Flight Ops flights show the same behavior. The firmware slides show VLife is a voltage-to-table calculation built from an unloaded battery. That names the SoC model as the mechanism; the 12% charger reading is a separate, less reliable indication.
notes: Split from VXEP-761; the 30 Oct smoke event (AS150 anti-spark melt from a poor battery mate) is a separate incident on another battery (SN 3-1351). The Root Cause field mixes both, its first bullet blaming AS150 damage, which the investigation itself says is unrelated to 12 Oct. The 12 Oct battery was SN 3-1353. The FW slides are mostly pictures with little text.

contributing: battery pack degraded to about 73% capacity after 44 flights

evidence.quote: there was a total energy consumption of 4.82Ah when the pack is rated to 6.6Ah (73% pack degradation
The vehicle was reading <21V (min cutoff voltage), but still reporting >25% SoC - this should never happen if the model was working.
Also, SoC continues to drop at the same rate after the vehicle landed indicating something is wrong with the model
The model might have some dependence on coulomb counting, which might be taking too much precedence on the SoC determination
Not enough info/priority to work on this.

team_view_in_comments: the vehicle is designed to accommodate for this degradation in its SoC model, but the model is failing to do so for whatever reason.

would_settle_it.what: SoC against pack voltage through landing, showing SoC still falling after touchdown
battery voltage, current and SoC channels to see whether the estimate follows coulomb count or voltage
how much weight coulomb counting gets against voltage in the SoC calculation

reasoning: The description, written by a battery engineer from the flight data, shows the vehicle reporting more than 25% SoC while pack voltage was below the 21 V cutoff, and SoC continuing to fall after landing. That places the fault in the vehicle SoC estimate rather than the pack, although the pack was also worn. The internal mechanism (coulomb counting precedence) is only a suggestion and was never checked; the ticket was canceled.
notes: Title is ambiguous ("B30 MB? HLB"), so it is not clear whether the pack was a main battery or an HLB. Tail 689 is taken from the AAR file name. Canceled for lack of information and priority. No converted attachments.

contributing: radio configurations never obtained from the customer
same symptom on VXE 729 and VXE 494 at the same site (VXEP-1047)
GCS mission simulation blocking uplink messages is a known cause of FWAP link faults (FS2-2332)

message occurs when the fixed wing autopilot does not receive messages from the GCS for more than 5 seconds during launch.
It’s hard to say specifically which part of the link failed without digging further into the data.
Could you request an export of the radio configurations from the GCS and the birds (729 and 498)?
Root cause believed to be GCS mission sim preventing uplink messages which trigger link timeouts resulting in log messages.

team_root_cause: Dropped Radio Link, possibly misconfigured radios

would_settle_it.what: XCOMM netS2P4RxComm uplink traffic and GCS event log at 18:36:11 to 18:36:16, to see whether the radio stopped passing data or the GCS stopped sending (for example a mission simulation)

reasoning: The event log shows the FWAP declared lost link during launch and triggered the abort, which per Jason Scherer means no GCS message for over 5 seconds. Nobody isolated which part of the GCS, radio, switch, XCOMM and serial chain dropped out, and the customer never supplied radio configurations. FS2-2332 shows GCS mission simulation can cause the same message, so a radio fault is the team's reading but not proven; this is a designed abort narrowed to the uplink.
notes: Split from VXEP-1047 (VXE 729); the customer said 498 flew with the 497 center wing and that 494 (with 503 CW) had the same aborts. Closed for lack of customer response. The six attached images are listed only.

team_view_in_comments: nothing to investigate here, just a procedural error.
reasoning: The battery was pulled from the engineering cabinet and left powering a vehicle for about an hour without a voltage check, ending at a few volts with heavy swelling. The engineer closing it called it a procedural error, and the linked ENG-2947 describes the same failure mode on VXE 797 with the same missing pre-use voltage check.
